reading_rules.text: Stage 4 starts from the observations, not the verses (researcher, #2526 Q7, 2026-11-21): the subgroups and the stage 3 observations on them are the input, the behaviours are discovered from analysing them, and the base data is read back into only occasionally. Every finding of step 3.1 or 3.2 rests on named observations (a traced node on each, with an occurrence node as well) and its occurrence nodes lie within the occurrences those observations cover; an occurrence outside them is allowed only where the finding records a read-back (the verse and why). Each node has a role from reading.node_roles other than lexical, chosen by the reading. A 3.3 finding carries nodes on the occurrences of both sides in the shared verses.

A finding of a stage 4 row is checked by the rules of observationrecord.check and check_item_parts (kind, text, basis, route, parts.item and what the item needs, node roles, collection of each node) and by RG, RW and RS, which are not restated here: one observation for each finding, never a duplicate, with a node on each word it applies to (RO11, RW-03); founded in the observations and never a restatement of the verse (B:131); parts.item is one of the items the row's item uses (cfg_setting layer.reading). An observation whose nodes all bear on an act is refused: those words are nodes of the observation of the act. A finding is a building block of a behaviour and never a claim (stage 5).

Nothing the step reads is lost on the way to stage 5. Step 3.1: every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared in not_used with its reason in words. Step 3.2: every 3.1 observation of the collection is gathered into a behaviour (a traced node on it from a flag finding of type discovery) or declared in not_gathered with its reason, and the row has at least one behaviour unless it is recorded as none with its reason. A behaviour names and gathers; it makes no claim about what the behaviour is.

An earlier inner-being observation with a node on the occurrences of a 3.1 row (any stage but lexical, layer-1, layer-2 and layer-3) is shown in the pull for information and may be actioned in `existing`: accepted, modified, deleted, merged or left, each with its reason, through observationrecord (RW-01, RW-09); nothing is demanded of it, and it counts for nothing in the check. A row answered again withdraws its earlier observations with the reason.
One observation per finding, never a duplicate description; a finding applying to several verses or words carries several nodes, each with the word's role in it.

Read outward from the verse, not inward from the scope's question. First record everything the verse carries, each with where it bears (chapter, thread, signpost); answer the scope's question last. A verse often has two or three significances, and none is dropped.
Read the verse in its passage and genre; name the speaker; explore figures for what they say about the inner being; take paired and opposite acts together. Restating a verse is not reading it.

Find the main inner-being operation, and give every word that bears on it its role in this finding (cfg_setting reading.node_roles): characteristic, qualifier and what it gives the characteristic, object or content, relational target, or enactment. A word read in the verse that holds nothing for the inner being is standalone. The role comes from this verse, never from the cluster tag. Where a standalone word proves to qualify a characteristic, it is a qualifier of it.

A qualifier gets no separate account of itself, but what it gives the characteristic it binds to is evaluated for its value and recorded as a qualification finding, applied by its nodes to the qualifier (role qualifier) and the characteristic (role characteristic). What it gives can vary widely: grade, nature, impact, size, relation, a measure, strengthening, ground, cause, object, setting or bait are examples, not a list (#2273 D9). A qualifier whose usage varies across contexts may earn its own reading later.
Record how the M-code words work together (a relational observation). Record any pointer outside the verse separately, without resolving it inline.

Record the parties: who bears the act, who causes it, who is acted on (source, target, impact, purpose), and the route (cfg_enum observation_route). A non-human being is never itself a HIB; a collective stays one HIB; an implied party is named as referential, never asserted.
Read the T3 operations, movement and force, negators (a refusal is an act), connectives, body parts, places, objects and nature for what they carry here; read every row, untagged ones too.

For every word that names an inner or bodily act, look at the original: the root's range in all three meaning sources read together, never one picked and the others dropped; the ESV renderings across its verses; whether the English adds or hides; the literal sense beside the rendering. Where more than one reading is open, record each, and mark the choice 'I read'.

Record each relevant word's face as it appears HERE: the circumstance in this verse and where the sense departs from the general gloss. Identifying and clarifying the face is lexical work; what the faces do for the inner being, and a double meaning in different scenarios, are layer 2 of the collection reading (layer-aspects-are-ledgered-and-never-left-open).
Never close a verse or item on 'not X'. A role label is never a verdict; the close records what the verse is. Silence about the inner being is a finding, recorded as data with its reason.
A phenomenon hidden behind a stated or refrained act may be named, with the verb, clause or stated silence that grounds it, and whether it is stated or read.
A literary or structural pattern is not an inner-being observation: log it as an open question instead. A human/divine comparison is recorded only where the text's own wording anchors it.
Keep the source of an interior state apart from the source of an enablement to act.
Morph is read, not carried: where occurrences of a word show different stems or voices, record whether the subject does, undergoes or causes the act.
A difference, or a specific inference, is its own observation, never folded into another.

A word that is only a homonym or a name, with no meaningful context, is recorded as such (tag no-human-context) and left. Data errors found while reading are flagged (tag data-error), not fixed in the reading.
The question catalogue's questions are prompts for the areas to explore. A question that does not apply is not answered, and no answer is manufactured beyond what the verse shows.
Faculty (heart, soul, spirit, mind) is reflected on at the end, over the scope, not per word.
Before reading the whole scope, read a few verses and have them checked.
No observation is changed except by a reading, and every change is recorded with its reason. An observation no longer supported by the verse is soft-deleted, with the reason.

A reading records findings of eight kinds (cfg_setting reading.observation_parts; the kind is the tag): face, qualification, party, statement, link, use, term, silence. A finding holds its text, meaning, implication, basis, its structured parts (ib_observation.parts: item, and mode, polarity, flag_type or grounds where its item needs them; reading.observation_items) and, on a party or link finding, its route; its nodes hold the verse, the word, the occurrence, the collection and its subgroup, the word's role in the finding and the reading that applied it. The silence kind is not used by Analysis_phase_1: a surface with no inner-being role is not recorded.
One observation per finding: the same description is never written twice. Applied to another verse, word or scope it gains a node on the existing observation.
Observation text is concise and tied to this verse's content, never a restatement of the word's dictionary sense. A transliteration is never given without its gloss.
An observation about a word can be answered only by consulting this occurrence's verse, span and morph.
Verse references are resolved fresh at write time, never taken from the text written. Relations are recorded only on evidence.

A flag raised in reading (needs adjacent context, a pointer) states its reason and what the follow-up must establish, and is carried to an open item, not resolved inline. Can't-resolve is recorded, never guessed (tag could-not-resolve).
Where the evidence points to more than one reading, each is its own observation with its own evidence.
A re-read includes the observations already recorded for the verse, so the reading sees prior findings and builds on them.
Where a verse ends up for a finding is recorded on the node (ib_node.disposition, cfg_enum observation_disposition: told, claim, held, data, context, withdrawn), with its reason or carrier.
Missing data in the base extract is named as a gap, never substituted from memory or outside knowledge.

After recording, every observation is read back against the verse for sense. An uncertain one is recorded as uncertain (tag could-not-resolve, or basis read: 'I read'), never asserted. A rule found to be systematically wrong is raised as a config change with the learning, never worked round in the reading.

A word is read per its lettered Strong's code (its grain), never the bare lemma (B:113). The occurrences of a word with several senses are related per grain and never aggregated across grains: related verses are same-grain occurrences.

Content words carry the inner-being impact and are read even when no cluster tags them. Function words (particles, prepositions, conjunctions, suffixes, pronouns) get no observation of their own, except negators and connectives, which are read for what they do (RG-07). A T2 word never stands alone: it is read as the qualifier of what it binds to.

The words in cfg_setting reading.non_characteristic_strongs are never a verse's characteristic: superscription metadata and named external adversaries. They are read as standalone or as qualifiers. The list is per word, not per cluster, because a cluster can hold both kinds.

A tagged word that works adverbially in an occurrence (a noun with a preposition qualifying the predicate, as 'in the counsel of the wicked') is a qualifier there, not the verse's characteristic. The role is per occurrence: the same word may be the characteristic elsewhere.
In a simile, the predicates of the vehicle (the tree that yields, does not wither) are read for what they say of the one compared (the tenor), not as the vehicle's own acts.

An existing observation counts for a surface when its node names that occurrence (verse_lexical_id), or, with none, when the node's verse, Strong and surface match one occurrence only. A node that names a verse and no surface, or matches more than one occurrence, is set aside: it does not count for any surface.

When a verse is worked, every existing observation and node on it, of any stage, is checked against the verse by its wording. The stage is not an indication of the nature of an observation and is never used to filter. Each observation is accepted, modified (changed in place; the old value, the new value and the reason are kept in ib_observation_change), soft deleted (the `deleted` column, with the reason), merged (a duplicate description, into the observation that is kept) or, when its wording shows it is not verse understanding, left exactly as it is with the reason. The check's fixes are part of it and need no separate approval. Nothing is physically deleted.

A surface with no inner-being role in a verse has no observation of its own. A word read in the verse that holds nothing for the inner being has the role standalone, which is a role and not an absence; where it could be a qualifier it is read as the qualifier of the characteristic it serves.

The observations of a verse state what the verse shows, and Record enforces it from cfg_setting reading.observation_rules and reading.observation_items: an observation of a relevant surface carries parts.item (one of the nine items), is written as one of the kinds that item allows, on a basis the item allows (a read observation names its grounds), and carries what its item needs (polarity, mode, flag type; a party carries its route). The words that bear on an act are nodes of the observation of the act, never an observation of their own (bears_on_only_refused). Every surface with the role characteristic has each applicable item observed or stated absent with the reason; the verse always has an operation observation. A verse whose observations do not comply is not recorded (#2329).

For every surface with the role characteristic, the nine items of spec 4.2 (reading.observation_items) are each explored, and each applicable item is its own observation (parts.item), written once and applied to every characteristic it is true of by its nodes; a qualifier or shared observation carries nodes on every characteristic it covers. An item the verse does not show gets no observation and is stated absent on the surface (items_absent) with the reason; the meaning item is never absent. The operation item carries a mode (done, foreseen, commanded, negated, reported) and an action description of who or what does what, read from before and after as the verse itself states them (passage-level before and after are the claims process's); the verse always has an operation observation. A read observation (basis read) names its grounds in the words of the verse (parts.grounds). No observation restates the verse text (no run of more than reading.observation_items max_verse_words_copied words). The same text for all items is not an exploration of them. Which word is the characteristic is the verse's decision, never the cluster's (RG-03). The nuance pointers (reading.nuance_pointers) say where each nuance is recorded (#2329).

rows.group: attending to a matter and turning it over
rows.asks: What do the stage 3 observations of this subgroup (its definition, its Strong's enrichment, its pairings, qualifiers, entities, direction, relations and double meanings, with the stage 1 senses) show of the elements of a behaviour of the inner being: what is done and its mode, whether a refusal or a pursuit, what it is directed at, the outward act, the other party with the route, the circumstance, the chain of operations, and the dimensions of the working (what a qualifier or a variation of the word gives it, from the lexical variation the stage 3 observations record)? Each finding is one observation that rests on named observations (a traced node on each) and carries nodes on the occurrences those observations cover, with the role each has; an occurrence outside them is allowed only with a read-back (the verse and why). Every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared not used, with the reason. A finding is a building block and never a claim about the behaviour as a whole (stage 5).

interventions: Work from the observations: the stage 3 observations of the subgroup are the input, and the verses are base data read back only where an observation does not settle the point; a read-back is recorded (the verse and why).
Read the lexical variation (the different Strong's codes of a surface, the forms of a word, the double meanings) as the dimensions of how the working happens, not as a difference to be smoothed away.
A behaviour is discovered from the elements, not assumed from the subgroup: a subgroup may form one behaviour, part of one, join others, or form none.

Record building blocks only. A statement of what a behaviour is, is a claim and belongs to stage 5; stage 5 receives the observations and not the subgroups, so everything it will need from them is recorded here.
Check the original where an observation depends on the word's range (RG-08); do not force a meaning and never close on 'not X' (RG-10).

A word whose role is not its collection's is reclassified by the collection change procedure and the step reopens (B:129, B:134); a discovery outside the observations is recorded as a flag finding of type discovery and is not resolved inline (RW-07).

Destruction stands with the group in Job 2:3 (destroy, 18 after), Psa 38:12 (ruin, 1 before) and Psa 119:78 (wronged, 3 before). In Psa 38:12 the ruin is 1 word before the meditating and the meditating is on treachery; in Psa 119:78 the speaker meditates after being wronged; in Job 2:3 the destroying is in a later clause.

Evil and the wicked stand with the group in Job 1:8 (evil, 12 after), Job 2:3 (evil, 13 after) and Pro 15:28 (wicked, 3 after). In Job the evil is what the one considered turns away from; in Pro 15:28 the wicked is set against the righteous whose heart ponders.

Fear stands with the group in Job 1:8 (fears, 9 after), Job 2:3 (10 after), Job 15:4 (fear, 2 before) and Mat 1:20 (14 after). In Job 1:8 and 2:3 the fear of God describes the one considered; in Job 15:4 fear of God and meditation are both what is being done away with.

Remembering stands with the group in Psa 63:6, Psa 77:3, Psa 77:6 and Psa 143:5, in every one 3 words before the member. The verses pair the remembering of God, a song or the days of old with the meditating that follows.

Precepts and authority stand with the group in Psa 119:15 (precepts, 1 after), Psa 119:27 (1 before), Psa 119:78 (2 after) and Mar 10:42 (exercise authority, 8 after). In the three Psalm verses the precepts are within two words of the meditating; in Mar 10:42 the member is the sense of those who are reputed rulers.

The heart stands with the group in five verses, within three words in every one: Psa 19:14 and Psa 49:3 (1 after, the meditation of the heart), Psa 77:6 (2 after), Pro 15:28 (2 before) and Luk 2:19 (3 after). The verses name the heart as the place of the meditating or pondering.

Works stand with the group in Psa 77:12 (work, 1 before), Psa 143:5 (work, 4 after), Psa 145:5 (works, 1 before) and Ecc 2:11 (toil, 4 after). In the three Psalm verses the works are God's and are the object of the meditating; in Ecc 2:11 the toil is the speaker's own.

Life and death stand with the group in Isa 53:8 (living, 5 after), Eze 18:28 (live, 8 after), Rom 4:19 (dead, 4 after) and Heb 11:19 (dead, 7 after). In Rom 4:19 and Heb 11:19 what is considered is a body as good as dead and God's power to raise the dead; in Eze 18:28 life is the outcome of considering and turning away.

Love stands with the group in Psa 119:48 (love, 1 before) and Psa 119:97 (3 before): in both the love of the commandments or the law comes just before the meditating on them. In Jos 7:21 the partner is covetousness (3 after) beside the surface 'weighing' as a weight of gold.

Searching stands with the group in Psa 38:12 (seek, 7 and 4 before), Psa 77:6 (search, 4 after) and Act 10:19 (looking for, 8 after). In Psa 77:6 the search follows the meditating in the same verse; in Psa 38:12 those who seek the speaker's hurt come before the meditating on treachery; in Act 10:19 the men looking for Peter are named after he is pondering.

Taking stands with the group in Gen 24:22 (took, 3 before), Jos 7:21 (took, 4 after), Eze 5:1 (take, 2 before) and Mat 1:20 (take, 15 after). In the first three the member is the weight of a thing taken (a ring, gold, balances), a measure and not a thought; only Mat 1:20, taking Mary as wife, belongs with the considering.

The surface 'considered' carries seventeen codes in two senses and some small words. Attention given to a matter: H7760K with H3820A (the idiom of setting the heart, Job 1:8 and 2:3, and Pro 24:32 with H7896K), H6437G (Ecc 2:11), H7200H (Eze 18:28), H7878 (Isa 53:8), H7920 (Dan 7:8), G1760 (Mat 1:20) and G2657 (Rom 4:19). Reckoning or being reckoned: H2803H (1Ki 10:21, 2Ch 9:20, Neh 13:13), H2803J

The surface 'meditate' carries three codes in three senses. Musing on a named object: H1897 (Jos 1:8, Psa 63:6, Psa 143:5), H7878 (nine Psalm verses, with Psa 77:3 as a complaint) and H7742 (Gen 24:63, the lexicon marks the meaning uncertain). Devising harm: H1897 in Psa 38:12, where the object is treachery. The same surface therefore gives a musing on God and the law, a complaint, and a plotting.

The surface 'meditation' carries five codes: H7881 (Job 15:4, Psa 119:97, Psa 119:99), H1902H (Psa 19:14), H1900 (Psa 49:3), H7879 (Psa 104:34) and H5921A (Psa 104:34, the preposition 'upon'). The four nouns give one sense, the inner musing; H7879 also lists 'complaint' in the lexicon but not in this verse.

The surface 'pondering' carries two codes, G4820 (Luk 2:19, to throw together, ponder) and G1760 (Act 10:19, to reflect on). The two Greek verbs give one sense, a sustained reflection on named things.

The surface 'ponders' carries two codes in two senses. H6424 in Pro 5:21 is the Lord's weighing of a man's paths, and H1897 in Pro 15:28 is a person's going over how to answer. The stored sense head of H6424 reads 'to envy' and disagrees with its lexicon range, flagged in #2533.

The surface 'weigh' carries three codes in two senses. Weighing out as a physical act: H8254 (Ezr 8:29, the vessels weighed before the priests) and H5187 (Zep 1:11, traders laden with silver). Weighing up what is said: G1252 (1Cor 14:29).

The surface 'weighing' carries two codes in two senses. H4948 (four occurrences in Gen 24:22 twice, Jos 7:21 and Eze 5:1) is a weight, a measure of shekels; H0239 in Ecc 12:9 is the Preacher weighing proverbs with care.

In Jos 1:8 the negator reaches 'depart' (the Book shall not depart), in Eze 18:28 it reaches 'die', in Mat 1:20 it reaches 'fear' (13 words after) and in Rom 4:19 it reaches 'weaken' (not the considering). The human are mostly the persons considered or doing the considering: the servant Job (4 with 'servant'), Solomon, Sarah, Isaac, Elijah, the priests Shelemiah, Zadok and Pedaiah, and 'man'. may_rest_on_besides.text: In Psa 1:2 hagah ('to meditate', literally to mutter) takes the law of the Lord as its object and day and night as its time: the one whose delight is in that law keeps occupied with it without ceasing, so the word names a continual dwelling on the written law.

In Pro 15:28 the righteous man's heart ponders how to answer him who asks, set against the wicked man's mouth that pours out evil: hagah ('to meditate, mutter') is the thinking that comes before speaking, done in the heart, so the answer is weighed before it is given.

In Gen 24:22, Jos 7:21 and Eze 5:1 mishqal ('weight') is a weight: a gold ring of half a shekel and two bracelets of ten shekels (Gen 24:22), a bar of gold of fifty shekels (Jos 7:21) and the balances for weighing the hair in the sign-act of Eze 5:1; in all four it is the weight of a thing, not an act of the mind.

In Mar 10:42 the participle of the verb 'to think' is used of those reputed to rule the nations; the sense is 'to be reckoned or held to be', a reputation held by others, and not the thinking of the subject, which is where this occurrence departs from the usual sense.

In Mat 1:20 the aorist participle of the verb 'to reflect on' states Joseph's deliberation over the matter before the angel appears; the lexicon's sense 'to revolve thoroughly in the mind, consider carefully' fits, and the object is the circumstances of Mary's pregnancy.

In Heb 11:11 and Heb 11:26 the verb whose first sense is 'to lead' is used of a judgment reached: Sarah judged the one who promised faithful, Moses counted the reproach of Christ a greater wealth; the sense in both is 'to esteem, count, hold to be', the lexicon's 'to think, consider, count'.

In Rom 4:19 the aorist verb of attentive observation has Abraham's own body as its object; the lexicon's sense 'to observe, consider thoroughly, with intense attention' fits, and the verse sets this looking at the facts beside his unweakened faith.

In Heb 11:19 the verb 'to reckon' is in the aorist middle participle and its object is a clause (that God was able to raise); the sense is to conclude by reckoning, reasoning to a conviction on the ground of God's character.

In Rom 4:19 the negator 'not' is stored in the unit of the surface 'considered' but the ESV verse states no negation of the considering: the 'not' in the verse bears on weakening in faith, and the negator sits beside the word, not on it; adjacency is not scope (LX-01). The occurrence is read as the negator it is, with the reach left to the verse.

In Dan 7:8 the Aramaic verb 'to be' (perfect, first person) is not a word of thinking: it stands with the participle of 'contemplate' (H7920) in the same verse and supplies the continued being-at-it of the looking, 'I was considering'; the dictionary sense 'to be, come to pass' is the helper here.

In 1Ki 10:21, 2Ch 9:20 and Neh 13:13 the Niphal of the verb 'to think, reckon' is passive: silver was not reckoned as anything in Solomon's days, and the men were reckoned reliable; the sense is 'to be accounted', the value or standing others assign.

In Pro 17:28 the Niphal imperfect, third masculine singular, means 'is reckoned' (a fool who is silent is reckoned wise); the standing is assigned from outside the person, by what others observe of his silence.

In Job 1:8, Job 2:3 and Pro 24:32 the noun 'heart' is the object-word of an idiom of setting the heart on something (the verbs set or put in the same verses, H7760K and H7896K), and the ESV renders the idiom as considered; the heart is the seat of the attention directed at Job or at the field.

In Ecc 2:11 the Qal of the verb 'to turn' is followed by the preposition and the objects of the speaker's work: the turning is a turning of attention toward them, and the ESV renders it considered; it is a physical verb used of directing the mind.

In Eze 18:28 the Qal narrative form of the verb 'to see' is the first of two acts (he considered, he turned away from the transgressions); the sense is 'to observe, consider', seeing taken in as grounds for the change of direction.

In Job 1:8 and Job 2:3 the verb 'to set, put' (perfect, second masculine singular) is joined with the noun heart in the same units: the idiom is 'set your heart', and it is what the Lord asks of Satan about Job; the physical verb of placing here directs attention.

In Isa 53:8 the Polel imperfect of the verb 'to muse' is put as a question about the speaker's generation: who gave thought to what happened to him; the sense is 'to reflect upon, take to heart', a deliberate musing that the generation did not do.

In Pro 24:32 the verb 'to set, put' (imperfect, first person) is joined with heart (H3820A, id 1281985 in the same verse): the speaker set his heart on what he saw in the field; it is the placing verb of the attention idiom, not a dictionary sense of thought.

In Dan 7:8 the Aramaic Ithpael participle 'contemplate' is the reflecting act of the speaker at the horns, carried with the helper verb 'to be' (H1934) in the same verse; the sense is attentive consideration.

In Pro 16:20 the Hiphil participle of the verb 'to be prudent' has the word (the instruction) as its object: the one who gives attention with insight to the word finds good; the sense is 'to give heed to with understanding', the lexicon's Hiphil 'to give attention to, consider'.

In Jos 1:8, Psa 63:6 and Psa 143:5 the verb 'to mutter, meditate' is used of reflection on an object the verse names: the Book of the Law by day and night, God on the bed, God's works of old; the sense is a repeated, quiet musing on that object.

In Psa 38:12 the same verb stands in a clause with speaking of ruin: those who seek the speaker's hurt meditate treachery; the object is deceit and the sense is devising harm, which departs from the musing on the Lord seen in the other three verses.

In Gen 24:63 the Qal infinitive 'to meditate' (the lexicon marks the meaning uncertain) states what Isaac went out to do in the field toward evening; the sense is quiet reflection while walking, set before the sight of the camels.

In Psa 77:6, Psa 77:12, Psa 119:15, 119:23, 119:27, 119:48, 119:78, 119:148 and Psa 145:5 the verb 'to muse' is used of the speaker's reflection on an object the verse names: his song, God's work and deeds, the precepts, statutes, promise and wondrous works; the sense is a deliberate pondering of that object.

In Psa 77:3 the same verb stands after remembering God and before the spirit faints; the lexicon lists 'to complain' for the Qal and the verse sets it with moaning, so it is musing that is a complaint, not a study of a named object.

In Psa 49:3 the noun 'meditation' (construct, with the heart) is set in parallel with the mouth's speech of wisdom; it is the inner musing of the heart, and the verse says its content will be understanding.

In Psa 19:14 the noun 'meditation' (construct, with the heart) is set in parallel with the words of the mouth and both are asked to be acceptable; it is the inner musing counterpart to speech, here chosen from the lexicon's 'meditation' over its 'resounding music'.

In Psa 104:34 the noun 'meditation' with the possessive stands as what the speaker offers and asks to be pleasing to the Lord; it is the musing as an offering, set before the speaker's rejoicing in the Lord.

In Job 15:4 the noun is the reflection before God that the speaker is accused of hindering; in Psa 119:97 and Psa 119:99 it is the law and the testimonies that are the speaker's meditation all day; the sense in all three is sustained reflection, whose object in the Psalm verses is the law.

In 1Ki 18:27 the noun 'musing' is the first of Elijah's mocking alternatives about the god (musing, relieving himself, journey, sleep); it names preoccupation, being occupied in thought, and is a mocking use that departs from the devout musing of the Psalm verses.

In Act 10:19 the present participle of the verb 'to reflect on' states Peter's continuing reflection on the vision as the Spirit speaks; the sense is sustained pondering of a given object (the vision), the lexicon's 'to ponder, reflect'.

In Luk 2:19 the present participle of the verb 'to throw together' is joined with treasuring up and with the heart: Mary brings the events together in her mind, which is the lexicon's 'to ponder'; the place is stated, in her heart.

In Pro 5:21 the Piel participle with the paths of a man as object means 'to weigh, make level', so the Lord weighs all his paths; the stored sense head 'to envy' for this code disagrees with the lexicon range (weigh, make level) and with the verse, and is flagged as a data error (RG-16), not corrected in the reading.

In Ecc 12:9 the Piel perfect of the verb 'to weigh' is the first of three acts of the Preacher in handling proverbs (weighing, studying, arranging); the lexicon lists 'weigh, test, consider', and here it is a careful judging of each proverb before it is set in order.

In 1Cor 14:29 the present imperative of the verb 'to distinguish, judge' is given to the others when two or three prophets have spoken: they are to evaluate what is said; the sense is 'to discern, judge' between the sayings.

In Zep 1:11 the adjective 'laden' (plural construct) describes the traders as those loaded with silver; the ESV renders it as weighing out silver, but the stored word is the adjective of being laden, not a verb of weighing.

In Ezr 8:29 the Qal imperfect of the verb 'to weigh' is the act of weighing the silver and the vessels before the priests, Levites and heads of fathers' houses; the sense is 'to weigh out' for an accounting, a physical weighing and not a mental one.

λογ-ίζομαι,

__2 with accusative et infinitive, reckon or calculate that.., λ. μύρια εἶναι [τὰ ἔτεα] [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__3 λ. τινί τι set down to one's account, οὗτος.. τὸ ἥμισυ τούτοις.. λελόγισται [Refs 5th c.BC+], compare 27; τἀνηλωμέν᾽.. οὐκ ἐλογιζόμην I did not charge them.., [NT+4th c.BC+]
__3.b audit the accounts of a person, with dative, τοῖς ὑπευθύνοις [Refs 4th c.BC+]
__II without reference to numbers, take into account, calculate, consider, ταῦτα [Refs 5th c.BC+]; λ. τι πρός τινας with them, [Refs 4th c.BC+]; also λ. περί τινος calculate, form calculations about.., [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.2 with accusative et infinitive, reckon, consider that.., τὸν ἕτερον [παῖδα] οὐκ εἶναί μοι λ. [Refs 5th c.BC+]; λ. ὅτι.. or ὡς.., [Refs 5th c.BC+]; ἐλογιζόμην πρὸς ἐμαυτὸν.., ὅτι.. [Refs 5th c.BC+]: with accusative et participle, Σμέρδιν μηκέτι ὑμῖν ἐόντα λογίζεσθε [Refs 5th c.BC+]: also with infinitive omitted, reckon or account so and so, τὸν καθ᾽ ἡμέραν βίον λογίζου σόν [εἶναι], τὰ δ᾽ ἄλλα τῆς τύχης [Refs 5th c.BC+]; πολὺν [εἶναι] τὸν κάτω χρόνον[Refs 5th c.BC+]; μίαν ἄμφω τούτω τὼ ἡμέρα λ. count both days as one, [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.3 with infinitive also, count or reckon upon doing, calculate or expect that.., ἐπισιτιεῖσθαι ἐλογίζοντο [Refs 5th c.BC+]; τί λογίζομ᾽.. προσδοκῶν χάριν παρὰ γυναικὸς κομιεῖσθα; [Refs 4th c.BC+]
__II.4 count upon, εἴ τις δύο ἢ καί τι πλείους ἡμέρας λ., μάταιός ἐστιν [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.5 conclude by reasoning, infer that.., with accusative et infinitive, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; λ. ὅτι.. [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.6 absolutely, τοὺς ἐπισταμένους λογίζεσθαι [Refs 4th c.BC+]; ὁ σπουδαῖος λελόγισται ἤδη has finished reasoning, [Refs 3rd c.AD+]
__III passive, mostly aorist ἐλογίσθην and (less frequently) perfect λελόγισμαι, also in present, participle λογιζόμενον [Refs 5th c.BC+], frequently in later Gr., [NT+3rd c.BC+]; χρήματα εἰς ἀργύριον λογισθέντα counted or calculated in silver, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; τὸ λελογισμένον, ={λογισμός}, [Refs 5th c.BC+]

lexicon.lsj:
οὐ,
the negative of fact and statement, as μή of will and thought; οὐ denies, μή rejects; οὐ is absolute, μή relative; οὐ objective, μή subjective. —The same differences hold for all compounds of οὐ and μή, and some examples of οὐδέ and οὐδείς are included below.—As to the Form, see infr. G. USAG[Refs 5th c.BC+]
__I as the negative of single words,
__II as the negative of the sentence.
__I οὐ adhering to single words so as to form a quasi-compound with them:—with Verbs: οὐ δίδωμι withhold, [Refs 8th c.BC+]; οὐκ εἰῶ prevent, [Refs]; οὐκ ἐθέλω refuse, [Refs]; οὔ φημι deny, [Refs 4th c.BC+]; but sometimes οὐ is retained, εἰ δ᾽ ἂν.. οὐκ ἐθέλωσιν [Refs 8th c.BC+]; ἐάντε.. οὐ (variant{μή}) φῆτε ἐάντε φῆτε [Refs 8th c.BC+] —On the use of οὐ in contrasts, see below [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II as negativing the whole sentence,
__II.1 οὐ is frequently used alone, sometimes with the ellipsis of a definite Verb, οὔκ (i.e. ἀποκερῇ), ἄν γε ἐμοὶ πείθῃ [Refs 5th c.BC+]: sometimes as negativing the preceding sentence, [Refs 5th c.BC+] and the accusative; sometimes without μά, οὐ τὸν πάντων θεῶν θεὸν πρόμον Ἅλιον [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.2 with indicative of statement, τὴν δ᾽ ἐγὼ οὐ λύσω [Refs 8th c.BC+]; οὐ φθίνει Κροίσου φιλόφρων ἀρετά [Refs 8th c.BC+]
__II.3 with subjunctive in future sense, only in Epic dialect, οὐ γάρ τίς με βίῃ γε ἑκὼν ἀέκοντα δίηται [Refs]
__II.4 with optative in potential sense (without ἄν or κεν), also Epic dialect, ὃ οὐ δύο γ᾽ ἄνδρε φέροιεν [Refs]
__II.5 with optative and ἄν, κείνοισι δ᾽ ἂν οὔ τις.. μαχέοιτο [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.6 in dependent clauses οὐ is used,
__II.6.a with ὅτι or ὡς, after Verbs of saying, knowing, and showing, ἐκ μέν τοι ἐρέω.. ὡς ἐγὼ οὔ τι ἑκὼν κατερύκομαι [Refs 8th c.BC+]: so with indicative or optative and ἄν, ἀπελογοῦντο ὡς οὐκ ἄν ποτε οὕτω μωροὶ ἦσαν [Refs 5th c.BC+] in such sentences, see at {μή} [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.6.b in all causal sentences, and in temporal and Relat. sentences unless there is conditional or final meaning, χωσαμένη, ὅ οἱ οὔ τι θαλύσια.. ῥέξε [Refs 8th c.BC+]: in causal relative sentences, οἵτινές σε οὐχὶ ἐσώσαμεν [Refs 5th c.BC+]; especially in the combinations, οὐκ ἔστιν ὅστις οὐ.., as οὐκ ἔστ᾽ ἐραστὴς ὅστις οὐκ ἀεὶ φιλεῖ [Refs 5th c.BC+]; οὐδείς ἐστιν ὅστις οὐ.. [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.6.c after ὥστε with indicative or optative with ἄν, ὥστ᾽ οὐ δυνατόν σ᾽ εἵργειν ἔσται [Refs 5th c.BC+]infinitive is almost invariably due to indirect speech, ὥστ᾽ οὐκ αἰσχύνεσθαι (for οὐκ αἰσχύνονται) [Refs 5th c.BC+]—Rarely not in indirect speech, [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.7 in a conditional clause μή is necessary, except,
__II.7.a in [Refs 8th c.BC+] clause precedes the apodosis and the verb is indicative, εἰ δέ μοι οὐκ ἐπέεσσ᾽ ἐπιπείσεται [Refs 8th c.BC+]
__II.7.b when the εἰ clause is really causal, as after Verbs expressing surprise or emotion, μὴ θαυμάσῃς, εἰ πολλὰ τῶν εἰρημένων οὐ πρέπει σοι [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.7.c when οὐ belongs closely to the next word (see. [Refs 4th c.BC+], or is quoted unchanged, εἰ, ὡς νῦν φήσει, οὐ παρεσκευάσατο [Refs 4th c.BC+]; εἰ δ᾽ οὐκέτ᾽ ἐστί (i.e. ὥσπερ λέγεις), τίνι τρόπῳ διεφθάρη ; [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.8 οὐ is used with infinitive in indirect speech, when it represents the indicative of orat. recta, φαμὲν δέ οἱ οὐ τελέεσθαι [Refs 8th c.BC+]; sometimes we have οὐ and μή in consecutive clauses, οἶμαι σοῦ κάκιον οὐδὲν ἂν τούτων κρατύνειν μηδ᾽ ἐπιθύνειν χερί [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.9 οὐ is used with the participle, when it can be resolved into a finite sentence with οὐ, as after Verbs of knowing and showing, τὸν κατθανόνθ᾽ ὁρῶντες οὐ τιμώμενον [Refs 5th c.BC+]; or into a causal sentence, τῶν βαρβάρων οἱ πολλοὶ ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ διεφθάρησαν νέειν οὐκ ἐπιστάμενοι [Refs 5th c.BC+]; or into a concessive sentence, δόξω γυναῖκα καίπερ οὐκ ἔχων ἔχειν [Refs 5th c.BC+] and participle, ὡς οὐχὶ συνδράσουσα νουθετεῖς τάδε [Refs 5th c.BC+]:—for exceptions, see at {μή} [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.9.b when the participle is used with the Article, μή is generally used, unless there is a distinct reference to a fact, when οὐ is occasionally found, ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς οὐκ οὔσης ἔτι [πόλεως] ὁρμώμενοι [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.10 Adjectives and abstract Substantives with the article commonly take μή (see. μή [Refs 5th c.BC+] is occasionally used, τὰς οὐκ ἀναγκαίας πόσεις [Refs 5th c.BC+]; τὴν τῶν γεφυρῶν οὐ διάλυσιν the non- dissolution of the bridges, the fact of their notbeing broken up, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; so without the article, ἐν οὐ καιπῷ [Refs]
__II.11 for οὐ μή, see entry
__II.12 in questions οὐ ordinarily expects a positive answer, οὔ νυ καὶ ἄλλοι ἔασι..; [Refs 8th c.BC+]; οὐχ ὁράᾳς..; dost thou not see? [NT+8th c.BC+]: the diphthong is genuine and always written ου (ουκ, ουδε, etc.) in early Inscrr., [Refs 4th c.BC+]; οὐ abbreviated ο, Suid. see at {Φιλοξένου γραμμάτιον}.
__H ACCENTUATION. οὐ is oxytone accusative to Hdn.Gr.1.494 (text doubtfulin 504): [Refs 8th c.BC+]
__H.I οὐ in connexion with other Particles will be found in alphabetical order, οὐ γάρ, οὐ μή, etc.—The corresponding forms of μή should be compared.

lexicon.lsj:
συμβάλλω,
future -βᾰλῶ: aorist -έβᾰλον, infinitive -βᾰλεῖν: perfect -βέβληκα: aorist 1 passive -εβλήθην:—of these tenses [Refs 8th c.BC+]present active, aorist active and middle, but most commonly Epic dialect intransitive aorist forms συμβλήτην, -βλήμεναι, middle σύμβλητο, -βληντο, -βλήμενος, subjunctive 2nd pers. singular -βλήεαι probably conjecture for -βλήσεαι in [Refs 8th c.BC+], 3rd.pers. singular contraction -βληται[Refs 8th c.BC+]:—throw together, dash together, σύν ῥ᾽ ἔβαλον ῥινούς, of men in close combat, [Refs 8th c.BC+]; bring together, unite, e.g. of rivers that fall into one another, ἐς μισγάγκειαν συμβάλλετον ὄβριμον ὕδωρ [Refs 8th c.BC+]:— middle, πολλοὶ ποταμοὶ σ. τὸ σφέτερον ὕδωρ [Refs 5th c.BC+]; ὁ Ἀκεσίνης τῷ Ἰνδῷ τὸ ὕδωρ σ. [Refs 2nd c.AD+]; σ. τὰ ὦτα πρὸς τὴν γῆν have their ears reaching to.., [Refs 4th c.BC+] —passive, κατὰ τὰς ῥᾶγας συμβεβλημένων [τῶν δακτύλων] [Refs 2nd c.AD+]
__2 collect, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; store up, accumulate, κριθὰς ἵπποις συμβεβλημένας πολλάς [Refs]
__3 jumble up together, διαφέροντα σ. εἰς ταὐτόν [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__4 intransitive in active, fit [Refs 4th c.BC+]; to be suitable, τὰ χεδροπὰ σ. εἰς τὰς νέας [Refs 4th c.BC+] (unless = sow, set).
__4.b to be profitable, σ. τῷ πολιτικῷ.. δικαίῳ εἶναι [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__5 intransitive, come together, ἔνθα δίστομοι.. σ. ὁδοί where two roads join, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; τὰ συμβάλλοντα the watersmeet, [Refs 3rd c.BC+]; [φλὲψ] σ. τῇ ἀποσχίσει [Refs 4th c.BC+]; collide, τοὺς τύπους ἀνάγκη συμβάλλειν ἑαυτοῖς [Refs 4th c.BC+]: Geometry texts, meet, τὸ σημεῖον, καθ᾽ ὃ συμβάλλουσιν the point in which (the straight lines) meet, [Refs 3rd c.BC+]
__6 βλέφαρα σ. ὕπνῳ close the eyes in sleep, [Refs 4th c.BC+]; how shall I meet her eyes with mine? [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__7 generally, join, unite, σ. σχοινία twist ropes (compare συμβολεύς), [Refs 5th c.BC+]; ὠμόλινον σ. πεντάπλουν [Refs 5th c.BC+]; fit together, ἁρμούς [Refs 4th c.BC+]; κεραῖαι συμβεβλημέναι [Refs 3rd c.BC+]; δεξιὰς σ. ἀλλήλοισι join hands, [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__8 σ. συμβόλαιά τινι or πρός τινα make a contract with a person, especially lend him money on bond, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; συμβόλαιον εἰς τἀνδράποδα συμβεβλημένον money lent on the security of the slaves, [Refs 4th c.BC+]: absolutely, in same sense, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; make a contract, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; of a marriage contract, Mitteis [Refs 2nd c.AD+]; advance, lend, πέρα μεδίμνου κριθῶν [Refs 4th c.BC+]; ἱμάτια, χρυσία, etc., [Refs 5th c.BC+]; ἐπί τισι on certain terms, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; ὁ συμβαλών the lender, creditor, [Refs 4th c.BC+]. the borrowers, debtors, [Refs]:— middle, with perfect passive, pay a share, contribute, ὁλκάδα οἱ συμβαλέεσθαι give him a merchant-vessel, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; σ. χρήματά τινι εἰς τροφὴν τῶν στρατιωτῶν advance it, [Refs 4th c.BC+]; τριήρεις εἰς κίνδυνον [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__9 generally, contribute:— passive, συμβάλλεταί τις.. μερίς [Refs 2nd c.AD+] —in this sense mostly in middle, τέμενος συμβάλλεσθαι add thereto, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; τὸ μὴ ἀγανακτεῖν.. ἄλλα τέ μοι πολλὰ συμβάλλεται, καὶ.. many circumstances contribute to my feeling no vexation, and especially.., [Refs 5th c.BC+]; τιμὴν καὶ δόξαν τῇ πόλει σ. [Refs 5th c.BC+]; frequently with μέρος as object, ἔργων οὐκ ἐλάχιστον μέρος σ. [Refs 5th c.BC+]; τὴν μεγίστην εἰς αὐτὰ μοῖραν [Refs 5th c.BC+] contributes to its volume, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; συμβαλλόμενα contributory causes, [Refs 4th c.BC+]: absolutely, to be helpful, πολλά ἐστι τὰ συμβαλλόμενα τοῖς βουλομένοις [Refs 5th c.BC+]; φόνου κηκὶς ξ. contributes to the proof, [Refs 4th c.BC+] many things contribute [their share] of this fear, i.e. join in causing it, [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__10 συμβάλλεσθαι γνώμας contribute one's opinion to a discussion, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; λόγον σ. περὶ βίου contribute an opinion about life, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; also συμβαλέσθαι τι to have something to say, [Refs]; ταῦτά σοι περὶ Ἔρωτος σ. [Refs]; συμβαλοῦ γνώμην contribute your opinion, help in judging, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; σ. τὴν γνώμην τῆς βουλῆς, with or without εἰς τὸν δῆμον, communicate it, [Refs]; cast votes, [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II συμβάλλειν (i.e. λόγους) converse, σ. τινί or πρός τινα, [NT+1st c.AD+]middle, ἀτὰρ τί ἐγὼ περὶ κλοπῆς σ.; [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II bring men together in hostile sense, pit them against each other, match them, ἀμφοτέρους θεοὶ σύμβαλον [Refs 8th c.BC+]; σ. σκύμνον λέοντος σκύλακι κυνός set one to fight with the other, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; ἄνδρα ἀνδρὶ καὶ ἵππον ἵππῳ σ. [Refs 5th c.BC+]; ἀλεκτρυόνας σ. [Refs 4th c.BC+] make him contend with.., [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.b middle, join in fight, σὺν δ᾽ ἐβάλοντο μάχεσθαι ἐναντίον [Refs 8th c.BC+]
__II.c intransitive, come together, σύμβαλον μάχεσθαι [Refs]; also ς. alone, come to blows, engage, πρίν γ᾽ ἠὲ ξυμβλήμεναι ἠὲ δαμῆναι [Refs 5th c.BC+]; Ἄρης Ἄρει δυμβαλεῖ, Δίκα Δίκᾳ [Refs 4th c.BC+]; Ἕλληνες Μήδοις σ. [Refs 5th c.BC+]; συμβάλλων coming into collision, [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.2 σ. πόλεμον καὶ δηϊοτῆτα engage in war, [Refs 8th c.BC+]; so in Trag., σ. βάκχαις μάχην [Refs 5th c.BC+] bandy reproaches, [Refs 5th c.BC+]
__II.3 middle, fall in with one, meet him, with dative, frequently in [Refs 8th c.BC+]aorist forms beginning ξυμβλη- or συμβλη- solely in this sense, Νέστορι δὲ ξύμβληντο [Refs 8th c.BC+]; ὅτε κεν συμβλήσεαι (to be read -βλήεαι) αὐτῷ [Refs 8th c.BC+]
__II.4 so in active, συμβαλών having met, [Refs 4th c.BC+]; οἱ συμβάλλοντες those who come in contact with one, [Refs 1st c.AD+]; φιλοσόφῳ σ. [Refs 2nd c.AD+]
__III compare, σμικρὰ μεγάλοισι [Refs 5th c.BC+]:—passive, [Refs 5th c.BC+]; τὸ ἀργύριον τὸ Βαβυλώνιον πρὸς τὸ Εὐβοικὸν συμβαλλόμενον τάλαντον the Babyl. talent being compared with, reduced to, the Euboic, [Refs]
__III.b compare for the purpose of checking, μέτρῳ συμβεβλημένῳ πρὸς τὸ χαλκοῦν Wilcken [Refs 3rd c.BC+]
__III.2 middle, reckon, compute, [Refs 5th c.BC+]:—passive, ἡ ὁδὸς ἡ ἡμερησίη ἀνὰ διηκόσια στάδια συμβέβληταί μοι [Refs]
__III.3 conclude, infer, conjecture, interpret, συμβαλεῖν τι [Refs 5th c.BC+]; σ. ὅτι.. [Refs 5th c.BC+]; τοῦτο σ. [Refs 5th c.BC+]; τοῦτο σ., ὅτι.. [Refs 5th c.BC+]; τὰ πρὶν οὐκ εὔγνωστα σ. [Refs 5th c.BC+]:—middle, absolutely, [Refs 5th c.BC+]: with accusative, make out, understand, τὸ πρῆγμα[Refs]infinitive, [Refs]
__IV agree, arrange, καθάπερ ξυνέβαλον ἢ διέθεντο [Refs 5th c.BC+]:—middle, make a treaty, Foed. cited in [Refs 5th c.BC+]; agree upon, fix, settle, λόφον εἰς ὃν δέοι ἁλίζεσθαι [Refs 5th c.BC+]

findings.text: Attending is a done act of musing on a named matter in Psa 1:2, Psa 63:6, Psa 143:5, Gen 24:63 and Pro 15:28 (how to answer), and of pondering in Luk 2:19, Act 10:19 and Mat 1:20 (the vision, these things). The verbs of musing and pondering are the same kind of act across the codes: a going over of something present to the mind, kept in the heart in Luk 2:19 and Pro 15:28.

The psalmist's meditating is foreseen as a resolve in Psa 77:12, Psa 119:15, 119:23, 119:27, 119:48, 119:78, 119:148 and Psa 145:5 (I will meditate). In seven of these the object is the Lord's precepts, statutes, promise, works or deeds, within two words of the member; the act is a purposed going over of what God has said or done.

Attending is commanded in Jos 1:8 (the Book of the Law is to be meditated on day and night) and in 1Cor 14:29 (the others are to weigh what the prophets say). The negator of Jos 1:8 reaches 'depart' (the Book shall not depart from the mouth), so the command to meditate stands beside a command that the Law not depart.

The Lord's own attending is stated in Job 1:8 and Job 2:3 (the Lord asks Satan whether he has set his heart on his servant Job) and in Pro 5:21 (the Lord weighs all a man's paths). The act is a looking at a person or a person's ways by the Lord, with Job as the object in the first two and the man's paths in the third.

Considering and counting as a done act appears in Neh 13:13 and 2Ch 9:20 (reckoned reliable, silver reckoned as nothing), Pro 17:28 (the silent fool counted wise), Heb 11:11, 11:19 and 11:26 (Sarah counting him faithful, Abraham concluding that God can raise the dead, Moses counting the reproach of Christ greater than treasures) and Mar 10:42 (those reputed to rule). The act is a judgment of standing or worth.

In 1Ki 10:21 the reckoning is negated: silver was not counted as anything in Solomon's days, and the negator reaches 'considered'. It is the only negated member of the group in the stored pairs that the negator reaches directly; in Jos 1:8, Eze 18:28, Mat 1:20 and Rom 4:19 the negators reach other verbs.
In 1Ki 10:21 the act is a refusal of worth: silver is counted as nothing, which the verse sets against the gold of Solomon's vessels.

Where the attending is of the law, God or his works it is a pursuit of its object: the love of the commandments comes within three words before the meditating in Psa 119:48 and Psa 119:97, and the psalmist's remembering stands 3 words before the meditating in Psa 63:6, Psa 77:3, Psa 77:6 and Psa 143:5. The attention is drawn toward what is loved or remembered.

The object of the meditating is the Lord's law and precepts in Jos 1:8, Psa 119:15, 119:27 and 119:78 (precepts 1 to 2 words from the member), his works and deeds in Psa 77:12, Psa 143:5 and Psa 145:5 (works 1 to 4 words), and the Lord himself and the days of old in Psa 63:6 and Psa 143:5. The object is God, what he has said and what he has done.

In Psa 38:12 the same verb of meditating has harm as its object: those who seek the speaker's hurt speak of ruin (1 word before) and meditate treachery, and in Psa 119:78 the speaker meditates on the precepts after he has been wronged (3 words before). The verb takes harm as its object in the first and is set against wrongdoing in the second.

The object of the considering is a person or the person's body in Job 1:8 and 2:3 (the servant Job), Rom 4:19 (Abraham's own body, as good as dead), Heb 11:11 (the one who promised), Eze 18:28 (the transgressions turned from), Ecc 2:11 (the work of his own hands) and Dan 7:8 (the horns). The objects are persons, bodies, deeds and the things seen in a vision.

The heart is named within three words of the member in five verses: 'the meditation of my heart' (Psa 19:14, Psa 49:3, each 1 word), 'in my heart' (Psa 77:6, 2 words), the heart of the righteous that ponders (Pro 15:28, 2 words before) and Mary pondering in her heart (Luk 2:19, 3 words). The verses place the attending in the heart.

Remembering stands exactly 3 words before the meditating in Psa 63:6, Psa 77:3, Psa 77:6 and Psa 143:5: the remembering of God, of a song or of the days of old comes first in the verse and the meditating follows it in the same sentence.

A second verb of musing stands in the same clause in Psa 77:12 (ponder, 3 before) and Psa 143:5 (ponder, 3 after), and the meditation of the heart is set between wisdom (1 before) and understanding (2 after) in Psa 49:3; in Pro 17:28 the silent fool is counted wise and intelligent. Wisdom and understanding stand beside the attending within four words in these verses.

Searching stands near the meditating in Psa 77:6 (search, 4 after, after the meditating), Psa 38:12 (seeking 7 and 4 before) and Act 10:19 (the men looking for Peter, 8 after the pondering). The search follows the attending in the first and the third and comes before it in the second.

Life and death are stated beside the considering in Eze 18:28 (the one who considers and turns away shall live, 8 after), Rom 4:19 (his body as good as dead, 4 after) and Heb 11:19 (raised from the dead, 7 after). In the last two what is considered is the state of death; in the first life is what follows the considering.

Fear and evil stand with the considering in Job 1:8 and Job 2:3 (the fear of God 9 to 10 words after, evil turned from 12 to 13 after), in Job 15:4 (fear of God and meditation both hindered, 2 words) and in Pro 15:28 (the wicked 3 words after the ponder). The attention of the Lord rests on one who fears God and turns from evil; the meditation is set beside what is done away with.

The nouns for meditation name the musing itself as a thing offered, loved or hindered: it is the meditation of the heart that is asked to be acceptable (Psa 19:14), that shall be understanding (Psa 49:3), that is asked to be pleasing (Psa 104:34), the law that is the speaker's meditation (Psa 119:97, Psa 119:99), and what is hindered before God (Job 15:4). Elijah's mockery names the god's musing (1Ki 18:27).

Weighing up as an evaluative act appears in Ecc 12:9, where the Preacher weighs proverbs with care and wisdom stands 6 words before; the physical weighing out of Ezr 8:29 is a counting of vessels before the priests. The evaluative weighing is one act of the attention of the Preacher among teaching, studying and arranging.

The surface 'weighing' is a weight in Gen 24:22 (twice), Jos 7:21 and Eze 5:1, a measure of shekels and not an act of the mind, and the surface 'weigh' is a physical weighing out in Ezr 8:29 and Zep 1:11 (laden); 'taking' stands beside the weights in the first three (took, 2 to 4 words). These occurrences are read as standalone: they are in the group because the surface also carries an evaluative use (1Cor 14:29, Ecc 12:9), and their placement was left as uncertain in the grouping.

The stored sense head of H6424 in Pro 5:21 reads 'to envy' against a lexicon range of weigh and make level (flagged in #2533), and the codes H0595 and H1934 in Pro 24:32 and Dan 7:8 are the pronoun I and a verb of being aligned into the units of 'considered'. They are not acts of attention; the verse acts are the verbs of setting the heart and contemplating beside them.
